_about: Step-slice cases (slice.py): one work item, run from step-plan to the end of its inner loop on a fixture repository. The prompt is the step's request; work_item is what the seed records as the plan's only item; checks run in a clean export of the product worktree's HEAD; expect_paths are fnmatch patterns the item's commits must touch. A case with a seeded_defect plants a latent defect its own checks do not exercise: probe commands (run by seeded_defects.py on the final tree, never part of the verdicts) fail when the defect survived, and tree names the reference trees under fixtures/ (naive: what a run with no review leaves; fixed: the corrected tree) that prove the probe tells them apart. Experiment cases (experiment.py, experiments.json) may add seed_records ({stage: fields} merged into the synthetic result of each stage the seed records, so a seed at test-spec carries a step plan), seed_state ({env, from}: a local target outside the checkout that keeps state, pre-loaded from a fixture; slice.seed_state), focused (the item's focused command an evaluator reruns) and stand_ins (fixtures/stand-ins/<case>/<name>: alternative implementations an evaluator swaps into the final tree).

sf-chess-engine.prompt: Build a chess rules engine in Apex with a simple Lightning web component board, in a Salesforce DX project in the current directory, and deploy and test it in the Salesforce Developer Edition org with alias `de`. Use `--target-org de` on every `sf` command that talks to the org; the CLI is already logged in, so never ask for, print or store credentials, and never run `sf org display` (it prints an access token). Name every Apex class `SLChess...` (for example `SLChessEngine`) and the component `slChessBoard`. Besides the Apex classes and the component, create exactly these kinds of metadata, all named with the prefix `SLChess`, so that the board opens in the org and the work can still be removed afterwards: a custom tab `tabs/SLChess_Board.tab-meta.xml` that is a Lightning component tab (`<lwcComponent>slChessBoard</lwcComponent>`; the component's meta file exposes the `lightning__Tab` target), a Lightning app `applications/SLChess.app-meta.xml` (standard navigation, containing that tab) and, if you want one, a Lightning app page `flexipages/SLChess_<Name>.flexipage-meta.xml` (then the component's meta file also exposes `lightning__AppPage`). Create no other metadata (no custom objects, fields, permission sets, static resources, triggers, profiles, labels or flows), and do not change profiles or permission sets. The Salesforce DX project root (`sfdx-project.json` and `force-app/`) is the current directory itself, not a subfolder. `SLChessEngine` is a public class with static methods only; a position is a FEN string. `startFen()` returns the standard start position. `legalMoves(String fen)` returns a `List<String>` of every legal move for the side to move in UCI form (for example `e2e4`, and `e7e8q` for a promotion), sorted alphabetically. `applyMove(String fen, String move)` returns the FEN after the move, with correct castling rights, en-passant square, halfmove clock and fullmove number, or throws `SLChessEngine.IllegalMoveException` (a public exception class you define inside `SLChessEngine`) when the move is not legal. The en-passant target square is set after every two-square pawn push, whether or not a capture is possible (the FEN-spec convention). `status(String fen)` returns `ongoing`, `check`, `checkmate` or `stalemate` for the side to move. Implement all piece moves, castling on both sides (never out of, through or into check; in UCI it is the king's two-square move: `e1g1`, `e1c1`, `e8g8`, `e8c8`), en passant, promotion to q, r, b or n, check, checkmate and stalemate. The component `slChessBoard` renders a FEN as an 8x8 board and is a game two people can play by turns on one screen: a person picks a piece and then a destination, the board shows whose turn it is and the game status (check, checkmate, stalemate), refuses an illegal destination, lets a pawn promote (queen is acceptable as the default) and has a New game button. It calls `SLChessController` and renders what comes back. `SLChessController` has `@AuraEnabled public static` methods `legalMoves(String fen)`, returning a `List<String>`, `applyMove(String fen, String move)`, returning the new FEN as a `String`, and `status(String fen)`, returning `ongoing`, `check`, `checkmate` or `stalemate` as a `String`, so that the grader can call them. The grader calls `SLChessController` only with legal moves and calls `SLChessEngine.applyMove` directly for an illegal one, so the controller may report an illegal move however suits the board (for example by throwing an `AuraHandledException`). The work will be graded by playing complete games, ply by ply, through `SLChessController` (`legalMoves`, `applyMove` and `status`), each game in one anonymous Apex run. Cover the rules with Apex tests in classes named `SLChess...Test` that run in the org, at least 8 Apex test methods in all: include known games (fool's mate, scholar's mate), castling, en passant, promotion, stalemate and move counts from standard test positions. Deploy with `sf project deploy start --target-org de` and run the tests in the org, one test class at a time, with `sf apex run test --target-org de --class-names <TestClass> --synchronous --result-format human --code-coverage` (a synchronous run takes one class). Keep the engine efficient enough that `legalMoves` on a middlegame position finishes well inside the synchronous Apex CPU limit, and so that a whole depth-2 legal-move enumeration (every legal reply to every legal move of a position, counted) runs inside one transaction, and so that a whole game of about 35 plies played through `SLChessController` (`legalMoves`, `applyMove` and `status` for every ply) does too. Do not stop until the tests pass in the org.

node-chess-engine.prompt: Build a chess rules engine as a Node.js module src/chess.js (CommonJS, no dependencies; npm test runs node --test). A position is a FEN string. startFen() returns the standard start position. legalMoves(fen) returns an array of every legal move for the side to move in UCI form (for example e2e4, and e7e8q for a promotion), sorted alphabetically. applyMove(fen, move) returns the FEN after the move, with correct castling rights, en-passant square, halfmove clock and fullmove number, or throws IllegalMoveError (a class the module also exports) when the move is not legal. The en-passant target square is set after every two-square pawn push, whether or not a capture is possible (the FEN-spec convention). status(fen) returns ongoing, check, checkmate or stalemate for the side to move. Implement all piece moves, castling on both sides (never out of, through or into check; in UCI it is the king's two-square move: e1g1, e1c1, e8g8, e8c8), en passant, promotion to q, r, b or n, check, checkmate and stalemate. Cover the rules with node --test tests in test/: known games (fool's mate, scholar's mate), castling, en passant, promotion, stalemate and move counts from standard test positions. Keep legalMoves on a middlegame position under 50 ms and a depth-2 legal-move count of the start position under 2 seconds. npm test must pass.

tickets-assign.about: E7 (docs/shiploop-test-stage-prompt-design-2026-10-30.md §7): the brownfield ticket-assignment case cut to one step, the assignment route without the listing filter and the command line. Its code introduces a name limit (at most 64 characters) and compound guards (only open and in-progress tickets), where 17 of 21 changed-line survivors of twelve Codex Terra brownfield runs were (docs/experiments/test-stage-prompt-20261030/brownfield-mutation.json).
tickets-assign.prompt: This directory is an existing Node.js service with no npm dependencies (README.md describes it): a help-desk ticket API, src/server.js, which `npm start` runs on the port in the PORT environment variable. Add ticket assignment. `PUT /tickets/:id/assignee` with a JSON body `{"assignee": "<agent>"}` assigns the ticket to that agent, and `{"assignee": null}` unassigns it; an agent is a non-empty name of at most 64 characters. Only open and in-progress tickets can be assigned or unassigned. Assigning a ticket to the agent it already has changes nothing. Every ticket shows its `assignee` (null when unassigned). The agent a ticket is assigned to is notified that it was assigned to them. Everything the service already does keeps working, and its existing tests must still pass as they are. Add node:test tests under test/ for the new behaviour; `npm test` runs them with the existing ones.
